la:noun:reatus.html:
rĕātus, ūs, m.
reus
.
Lit., the condition of an accused person, a state of impeachment (a word first used by Messala, acc. to ): revocato ad reatum Alcibiade,: si diutino tempore aliquis in reatu fuerit ... qui longo tempore in reatu agunt,; .—
Meton.
An offence of which one stands accused, a charge, ; , p. 132, 10; .—
The dress or appearance of an accused person: mulier reatu mirāque tristitie deformis,.—
Trop., guilt (late Lat.): reatus sanguinis,; cf. : praeteriit actu manet reatu, Aug. cont. Jul. Pelag. 6, 19, 60.

la:verb:reaedifico.html:
rĕ-aedĭfĭco, āre, v. a.,
to build again, rebuild (late Lat.): reaedifico quae destruxit,; so ; ; .

la:adv:reapse.gloss: in reality; in fact; in practice
senses: in reality; in fact; in practice
la:adv:reapse.html:
rēapse, adv.
contr. from re and eapse, an old form for ipsā; hence in tmesi: reque eapse, Scip. Afr. ap. ; cf. ipse init.
,
in fact, in reality, actually, really (an old word, which does not occur after Cic.): reapse est re ipsā, Müll.; : earum ipsarum rerum reapse, non oratione perfectio,: ut reapse cerneretur, quale esset id, quod, etc.,; cf. : obiciuntur etiam saepe formae, quae reapse nullae sunt, speciem autem offerunt,: non perinde, ut est reapse, ex litteris perspicere potuisti,: quod idem reapse primum est,.
